worksheet.title: Start It, Then Repeat
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.1 — events + repeating
worksheet.learning_goal: I can use an event to start a loop that repeats.

parts.title: What starts the code?
text: Think of an alarm going off — that is what STARTS your morning. In code, an event block (like "when the green flag is clicked") starts a script.
After the event starts it, a repeat loop can run again and again. The event is the GO signal; the loop does the repeating. Bit will show you.

parts.title: Read this script
parts.note: Clicking Bit is the EVENT that starts the script. Then the loop repeats the inside 3 times.

parts.caption: The event is the GO signal; the loop does the repeating.

parts.title: Count it
parts.prompt: In the script above, the event starts the loop. The loop says repeat 3. How many times do the inside blocks run? ______

parts.title: Predict, then check
parts.prompt: You change "when this sprite clicked" to "when green flag clicked". The loop is the same. PREDICT: what is different now — WHAT do you do to start it? Write your answer.

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Make Bit spin 4 times when the SPACE key is pressed. Fill in the blanks:  when ______ key pressed → repeat ______ → ( turn )

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit has: when flag clicked → repeat 5 → ( move ). If you click the green flag ONCE, how many moves? If you click it TWICE? Explain why.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: An event block STARTS the code. The loop inside it does the repeating. Fire the event again and the loop runs again.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: An event block starts a script, and a repeat loop inside does the repeating. Students count the loop, change the event, write their own event-and-loop, and reason about starting the event twice. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the blocks and what Bit does, so you can teach from the printout. Optional: a Scratch-style app to drag the blocks and watch Bit run — you only press the green flag.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). The event (clicking Bit, or the green flag) starts the script; the repeat loop inside does the repeating.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — the inside blocks run 3 times.
3. Let them work. Students change the event (Ex 2), write an event-and-loop (Ex 3), and reason about two clicks (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — 3 times. Exercise 2 — now you start it by clicking the green flag instead of clicking Bit (the loop runs the same).
Exercise 3 — when SPACE key pressed → repeat 4. Exercise 4 (challenge) — one click = 5 moves; two clicks = 10 (the event starts the loop each time).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: thinking the event changes how many times the loop runs. The event only starts the script; the repeat number sets the count.
Make it easier: point to the event on top, then the repeat inside.
Make it harder: ask how many moves three clicks of a repeat-5 loop give (15).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child sees the event starts the script and the repeat sets the count, and reasons about firing it twice.
